entities.name: Meng Ao
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Meng Ao (d. 257 BCE) was a prominent general of the State of Qin during the tumultuous Warring States period (475–221 BCE) in ancient China. His military prowess and strategic acumen were instrumental in Qin's relentless territorial expansion, laying the groundwork for its eventual unification of China under Qin Shi Huang. He served under King Zhaoxiang of Qin and King Xiaowen of Qin, participating in numerous campaigns that systematically eroded the power of rival states such as Han, Wei, and Zhao, demonstrating the strategic vision and military might that would come to define the Qin dynasty.

Meng Ao's career was marked by a series of decisive victories that significantly expanded Qin's dominion. In 276 BCE, he led Qin forces to conquer the strategic city of Qi in the State of Wei, reportedly capturing over 100,000 enemy soldiers, a staggering number for the era. Two years later, in 274 BCE, he again attacked Wei, seizing the important cities of Yan and Ancheng. Perhaps his most impactful campaign occurred in 268 BCE, when he launched a major offensive against the State of Han, capturing Zheng (present-day Xingyang, Henan) and further weakening one of Qin's primary adversaries. These conquests were crucial for securing fertile lands, strategic passes, and vital resources for Qin.

The campaigns spearheaded by Meng Ao, alongside other formidable Qin generals like Bai Qi and Wang Jian, systematically dismantled the military capabilities and territorial integrity of the other Warring States. His conquests contributed directly to Qin's strategic dominance, paving the way for the later, more extensive unification campaigns orchestrated by Qin Shi Huang. Meng Ao's military achievements exemplified the ruthless efficiency and strategic foresight that characterized Qin's rise, establishing precedents for centralized military command and territorial consolidation that would profoundly shape the future of imperial China.
